title: Annotatio IV §.X close: Vigilius — natural local absence; two natures — stop before §.XI
pass_a_gloss: whose words disputing against Eutyches and Nestorius, most worthy of note, set out the whole sentence of the Reformers on this matter: The Son of God, he says, according to humanity withdrew from us; according to divinity He is with us: Behold I am with you. By the form of a servant, which He took away from us into heaven, HE IS ABSENT FROM US; by the form of God, by which He does not withdraw from us, He is present to us on earth (Book 1). Likewise Book 4: The flesh of Christ, when it was on earth, was certainly not in heaven, and now because it is in heaven, IT IS CERTAINLY NOT ON EARTH. It appears that one and the same Christ IS OF BOTH NATURES, and is indeed everywhere according to the NATURE of His divinity, and is contained in a place according to the NATURE of His humanity.
pass_b_english: Vigilius (against Eutyches and Nestorius) states the Reformers’ sentence: according to humanity the Son withdrew; according to divinity He is with us.

By the servant-form taken into heaven He is ABSENT; by the form of God He is present on earth. Flesh once on earth was not in heaven; now in heaven it is NOT ON EARTH. One Christ of BOTH NATURES — everywhere by divinity, place-bound by humanity.
source_text: cujus contra Eutychen & Nestorium disputantis verba notatu dignissima, omnem hac de re sententiam Reformatorum exponunt: Dei filius, ait ille, secundum humanitatem recessit à nobis, secundum divinitatem ait nobis: Ecce ego vobiscum sum. Per formam servi, quam abstulit à nobis in cælum, ABSENS EST NOBIS; per formam Dei, qua non recedit à nobis, in terris præsens est nobis, Lib. 1. Itemque Lib. 4. Caro Christi, quando in terra fuit, non erat utique in cælo, & nunc quia in cælo est, NON EST UTIQUE IN TERRA. Apparet unum eundemque Christum, UTRIUSQUE ESSE NATURÆ, & esse quidem ubique, secundum NATURAM divinitatis suæ, & loco contineri, secundum NATURAM humanitatis suæ.
